p: The KJV's "the second sabbath after the first" translates a puzzling Greek word that the oldest manuscripts do not have.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; Papyrus 4 and Papyrus 75 (about AD 200), Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), and others, as reported by Metzger
Codex Alexandrinus (400s), Bezae (400s), the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The word deuteroprōtos, "second-first," is found nowhere else in Greek literature, and no one knows what it means. The earliest witnesses lack it, and it is easier to explain how it got in than how it would have dropped out: a scribe may have written "first" in the margin to match "another Sabbath" in 6:6, another wrote "second" with 4:31 in mind, and a copyist combined them.
b: Guesses at a meaning include the first Sabbath after the second day of Passover (counting toward Pentecost, Leviticus 23:15), the first Sabbath of the second year of a cycle, or the second Sabbath of the first month. Jerome tells how he asked his teacher Gregory of Nazianzus what the word meant, and Gregory joked that he would explain it in church, where the people's applause would force Jerome to agree (Jerome, Letter 52.8).

a: Then he told them, "The Son of Man is Lord over the Sabbath."
t: The man working on the Sabbath
p: Codex Bezae moves this verse after 6:10 and puts here a saying of Jesus found in no other Gospel manuscript.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and nearly all manuscripts
readings.orig: καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Κύριός ἐστιν τοῦ σαββάτου ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.
readings.en: And he said to them, The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
readings.plain: Then he told them, "The Son of Man is Lord over the Sabbath."

readings.w: Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς ὅτι Κύριός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τοῦ σαββάτου.
readings.en: And he said to them that the Son of Man is Lord also of the Sabbath.
readings.plain: Then he told them, "The Son of Man is Lord even over the Sabbath."

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, 400s) alone, which places the usual 6:5 after 6:10
readings.orig: Τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ θεασάμενός τινα ἐργαζόμενον τῷ σαββάτῳ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἄνθρωπε, εἰ μὲν οἶδας τί ποιεῖς, μακάριος εἶ· εἰ δὲ μὴ οἶδας, ἐπικατάρατος καὶ παραβάτης εἶ τοῦ νόμου.
readings.en: On the same day, seeing someone working on the Sabbath, he said to him: Man, if you know what you are doing, you are blessed; but if you do not know, you are cursed and a transgressor of the law.
readings.plain: On the same day he saw a man working on the Sabbath and said to him, "Man, if you know what you are doing, you are blessed. But if you do not know, you are cursed and a breaker of the Law."

why: Every other manuscript has the saying about the Son of Man here, and Bezae is known for adding and rearranging material in Luke and Acts. The Byzantine wording adds "also" (Mark 2:28's word) and moves it; the meaning is the same.
b: The Bezae saying is one of the best-known agrapha, sayings of Jesus outside the canonical Gospels. Joachim Jeremias thought it might be genuine: it fits Paul's teaching that whatever is not done from faith is sin (Romans 14:23) and that a person who acts with a clear conscience is free. Most scholars think it is an early tradition that a scribe of the Bezae line inserted, and few think Luke wrote it. It is not Scripture in any church.

p: A few manuscripts read "despairing of no one" instead of "hoping for nothing in return."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
Codex Sinaiticus (01), W, Ξ and the Old Syriac, as reported by Metzger

why: The difference is a single letter (μηδέν / μηδένα). The verb apelpizō usually means "to despair," and some scribes read the line that way; but with "lend" the sense "expect back" fits, and most witnesses have mēden. The Latin Vulgate's nihil inde sperantes, "hoping for nothing from it," became the church's main proof text against lending at interest (see the note on 6:34).

t: "Let him be healed" or "he will be healed"?
p: The KJV's "my servant shall be healed" follows the future tense, as in Matthew 8:8. The modern editions print a command.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott and Hort, Tregelles; Papyrus 75 and Codex Vaticanus, with a few others
Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Bezae and most later manuscripts (the Byzantine majority); Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: This is one of the places where the editors follow Papyrus 75 and Vaticanus against most early manuscripts. The future may have come in from Matthew 8:8, which has iathēsetai; copyists often made Luke match Matthew, and the less familiar wording is the likelier original. The sense is close either way: the centurion trusts Jesus' word to heal.

p: One letter decides whether Jesus came to Nain "soon afterward" or "the next day" (KJV).

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott and Hort, Tregelles, and the Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV) and a number of manuscripts, some of them early (the witnesses are not checked here against the NA28 apparatus)

why: With the masculine or neuter article (tō) the phrase means "afterward"; with the feminine (tē, agreeing with an unstated "day") it means "the next day." All the modern editions and the Byzantine text read tō. Nothing in the story depends on it.

p: The KJV begins this verse "And the Lord said," words found in hardly any Greek manuscript.

p: Codex Vaticanus reads "the prophet," as if Simon meant the promised Prophet like Moses.

why: With the article Simon would be weighing whether Jesus is the expected Prophet of Deuteronomy 18:15 (compare John 1:21; 6:14). Most witnesses lack it, and the general sense "a prophet" fits 7:16. A copyist may have added it under the influence of John's Gospel.

p: Did the women support "them" (Jesus and the Twelve) or "him" (Jesus)? The KJV has "him."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; Codex Vaticanus, Bezae, W, the Byzantine majority, as reported by Metzger
Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and others; Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: "Him" matches Mark 15:41 and Matthew 27:55, which say the women served Jesus, and it focuses on Jesus; Metzger judged it a change by copyists who wanted the women's service to be to the Lord. "Them" includes the Twelve and makes the women patrons of the whole mission.

p: Manuscripts of all three Gospels disagree about the place name. Luke's best witnesses have Gerasenes, as Mark's do.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; Papyrus 75, Codex Vaticanus, Bezae, the Latin versions, as reported by Metzger
Codex Sinaiticus, L, Θ and others, as reported by Metzger
Codex Alexandrinus, W, the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: Gerasa (modern Jerash in Jordan) was a great Decapolis city about 33 miles (53 km) from the lake; Gadara, about 6 miles (10 km) away, owned land reaching toward the shore; Gergesa may be a small place on the shore (often linked with Kursi), a name Origen promoted because the other two seemed too far. Gerasenes has the earliest and most varied support in Luke and Mark; Gadarenes is the best reading in Matthew 8:28. The Plain follows the same reading as at Mark 5:1.
b: See also the variant at 8:37, where the same names appear, and the notes at Mark 5:1 and Matthew 8:28.

why: The evidence is closely balanced.
